Employment Scams

Work From Home Scam UK: Envelope, Kit & Reshipping Cons

An upfront starter-kit, materials or registration payment is a scam warning; verify the role, business and fee before paying.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-04-22 · Updated 2026-07-30 · 6 min read

Quick answer: A home-working job that asks you to pay for a starter kit, materials or registration before you have earned anything is a scam warning. Agencies generally cannot charge individual applicants for finding work. Be wary of parcel-reshipping jobs. Report suspected fraud to Report Fraud or Police Scotland on 101.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What a classic work-from-home scam looks like

This scam is an advert offering home-based work — envelope-stuffing, product assembly, or "running your own business" — that asks you to pay upfront for a starter kit, materials, or registration before you can begin. An example of the style: Earn £300/week stuffing envelopes from home. Send £45 for your starter kit to begin. A second, distinct version recruits you to receive and repost parcels for a company, without making clear that the goods may be linked to fraud. Requests to pay before earning and unexplained parcel handling are warning signs; the employment-agency fee rules are set out below.

Why it's convincing

Genuine home-based work and small businesses do exist, and the appeal of flexible earning is real. The upfront fee is often framed as a small, reasonable cost for materials or training rather than a red flag in itself. In the reshipping version, you may not realise anything is wrong until well after you've agreed to help.

Signs a work-from-home offer is a scam

  • You're asked to pay upfront for a "starter kit", materials, registration, customer leads, or instructions before you can start earning.
  • You complete work but the supposed business avoids paying you for it.
  • You're asked to receive parcels at your home address and repost them elsewhere.
  • You're promised a specific weekly income for running "your own business" from home.
  • The company has no verifiable registration or presence beyond the advert itself.

How the scam works step by step

In the kit-fee version: first, an advert promises easy, flexible home-based earnings; second, you pay upfront for a starter kit or materials; third, either the kit is worthless or the supposed business avoids paying you for work you have done, and the fee is gone.

In the reshipping version, a supposed employer asks you to accept parcels at home and forward or redirect them. Lincolnshire Police warns that criminals use parcel-mule tactics to move goods and avoid detection, and lists requests to store, forward or redirect parcels as warning signs. Stop and verify before accepting or forwarding anything you cannot independently account for.

How to check a work-from-home offer safely

Treat an upfront payment to secure work as a serious warning sign. For most individual applicants, agencies cannot charge for finding work. The main sector exception covers specified entertainment and creative occupations, photographic or fashion modelling, and professional sport; separate rules can apply to some incorporated work-seekers and publication-only services. Home-working, assembly and envelope work are not in that sector exception. Our recruitment agency scam guide explains the detail, including why a genuinely optional service unrelated to work-finding may be charged for only when buying it is not a condition of finding work.

A fee that can be genuine is a criminal-record check, which is a different thing from being charged to find work. An individual can apply directly for a basic DBS check in England or Wales, a Level 1 disclosure in Scotland, or a basic AccessNI check in Northern Ireland; higher levels — including Level 2 and most PVG applications — are restricted to eligible roles and are started by an employer, organisation or registered body. Check the level, route and current fee on that service rather than paying a recruiter or a private account.

  • Research the company independently before paying anything or agreeing to receive parcels on its behalf.
  • Be especially wary of any "job" that asks you to handle parcels, or to receive, hold, convert or forward someone else's money through an account in your own name.
  • If promised payment for completed work never arrives, stop before paying another fee and report the offer.

If you've already paid a fee or are reshipping parcels

If you are currently receiving and reposting parcels, stop immediately and get independent advice before handling anything else. If you paid an upfront fee by card, contact your bank or card provider about a chargeback; a Section 75 claim may apply where the credit-card cash price was more than £100 and no more than £30,000. If money belonging to someone else has passed through your account, tell your bank the same day and read the National Crime Agency's money-muling guidance. Our scam recovery checklist sets out the order.

How to report a work-from-home scam (UK)

Report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. For an SMS, forward the message to 7726. For WhatsApp, Telegram or Signal, preserve the evidence and use the app's report and block tools; 7726 is not the in-app reporting route. A suspicious email can go to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk.

Frequently asked questions

Are envelope-stuffing and home-assembly jobs ever genuine?

Classic "earn money from home" adverts of this style are high-risk. Genuine home-based work shouldn't require you to pay an upfront fee for a vague kit or materials before you can start.

What is reshipping and why is it dangerous?

It is when a supposed employer asks you to receive parcels at home and repost them elsewhere. Police warn that criminals can use these parcel-mule tactics to move goods and avoid detection. Stop and verify before accepting or forwarding anything you cannot independently account for.

I've already paid for a work-from-home starter kit — what do I do?

Contact your bank or card provider about a chargeback and report the company; a Section 75 claim may apply where the credit-card cash price was more than £100 and no more than £30,000. If you paid by bank transfer, the APP reimbursement rules can cover an eligible domestic consumer payment dated 7 October 2024 or later and sent by Faster Payments or retail CHAPS: the limit is £85,000, the claim must come inside 13 months, exclusions apply, and an excess of up to £100 may be taken off — but not from a consumer the firm assesses as vulnerable. None of it is a guaranteed refund.

I've been reposting parcels for a company I now think is a scam — am I at risk?

Stop immediately, don't accept or repost any more parcels, keep any records you have, and report what has happened. Get independent advice from your nation's consumer service — Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262 — before agreeing to anything else, and tell your bank the same day if money as well as parcels passed through your hands.

How do I report a work-from-home scam?

Report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Forward a suspicious text to 7726, and use the app's own report and block tools for a WhatsApp, Telegram or Signal message.
